name: Demons
description: A cross-cultural class of supernatural beings, generally malevolent or morally ambivalent, found in nearly every major religious and folkloric tradition. The Christian-Islamic concept of demons as evil spirits or fallen angels developed from older Greek, Hebrew, Mesopotamian, and Zoroastrian categories of intermediate spirits.
full_description: A demon is, broadly, a supernatural being whose function in a religious or folkloric system is to harm, tempt, or oppose humans, the divine order, or both. The English word descends from Greek δαίμων (daimōn), originally a morally neutral term for an intermediate divine being between gods and humans, used by Hesiod, Plato, and the Pre-Socratics. Hellenistic and early Christian writers narrowed the term to malevolent spirits, conflating it with Hebrew shedim and se'irim and with the fallen-angel traditions of Second-Temple Jewish apocalyptic literature (1 Enoch, Jubilees). Christian theologians (Augustine of Hippo, Aquinas) systematised demons as fallen angels under Lucifer/Satan; medieval and Renaissance demonology produced extensive hierarchies (Pseudomonarchia Daemonum, 1577; Lesser Key of Solomon, 17th century) and lists of named demons (Asmodeus, Belial, Beelzebub, Astaroth, Belphegor). Islamic tradition distinguishes shayāṭīn (devils, with Iblīs as their head) from jinn (a separate created order with free will, capable of being good or evil). Zoroastrianism inverts the older Indo-Iranian deva/asura distinction so that the daēvas become demons under Angra Mainyu. Hindu cosmology recognises asuras and rākshasas, and Buddhism the māras and naraka-beings, but in both traditions such beings are subject to karma and rebirth rather than being eternally damned. Folkloric demons appear in Mesopotamian texts (utukku, Lamaštu, Pazuzu), in Japanese tradition (oni, yōkai), and across many other cultures.
origin: Demonology is a near-universal feature of human religious systems, with major systematised traditions in West Asia, Europe, North Africa, South and East Asia.

etymology.origin: Greek δαίμων (daimōn), of disputed root: possibly from δαίεσθαι 'to divide, distribute', i.e. 'distributor of fates'. The Latin daemon was theologically narrowed to evil spirits in patristic and medieval Christian usage.
etymology.meaning: In classical Greek, an intermediate divine being or guardian spirit; in later Christian theology, an evil supernatural being or fallen angel.
etymology.first_use: Greek daimōn attested in Homer (8th century BCE) and Hesiod; the narrow 'evil-spirit' sense crystallises in Greek-Jewish and Christian texts of the Hellenistic and early imperial periods.

timeline.event: Mesopotamian demonological literature: utukku, gallu, Lamaštu, Pazuzu in Sumerian and Akkadian incantations
Zoroastrian Gathas and later Avestan literature relegate the daēvas to demonic status
1 Enoch and Jubilees (3rd–2nd centuries BCE) develop the fallen-angel tradition (Watchers)
timeline.significance: Bridge between Hebrew Bible and later Christian/Islamic demonology

timeline.event: Augustine of Hippo's De Civitate Dei integrates Greek daimones into Christian demonology
timeline.significance: Shapes Latin Christian demonology for a millennium

timeline.event: Thomas Aquinas systematises Catholic angelology and demonology in the Summa Theologiae
Heinrich Kramer's Malleus Maleficarum (1486) institutionalises the witchcraft–demonology connection
Johann Weyer publishes Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (appended to De Praestigiis Daemonum)
Roman Catholic Rituale Romanum (1614) standardises the rite of exorcism
William Friedkin's The Exorcist (Warner Bros.) opens in U.S. cinemas
timeline.significance: Reignites Western popular interest in demonology and exorcism

timeline.event: Vatican issues revised rite of exorcism (De Exorcismis et Supplicationibus Quibusdam)

cultural_notes: Belief in demons remains widespread across Christianity, Islam, and many other faiths. Practical responses include prayer, sacramentals, exorcism, ruqyah, mantra, talismans, and other apotropaic practices.
